Testimony in Support of LD 193 - "An Act to Fund Students in Maine Schools Who Are Experiencing Homelessness"
Feb. 26, 2025
Senator Rafferty, Representative Murphy, and distinguished members of the Committee on Education and Cultural Affairs, I am Cara Pelletier, City Council Chair for the City of Bangor, and I am providing testimony in support of LD 193, "An Act to Fund Students in Maine Schools Who Are Experiencing Homelessness."
Across Maine, more communities are seeing residents unable to find a permanent place to live, largely because of the affordable housing crisis, and our schools sit on the front lines of this challenge.
During the last school year, more than 4,000 Maine students lacked a fixed place to live each night - doubled-up with friends or staying in a hotel. Every day our staff see more students enter class without basic items like clean clothes, hygiene products and school supplies.
It's heartening to see that the Legislature has taken steps to tackle this growing challenge. The recent pilot program sponsored by Sen. Rafferty to provide up to $750 per student for emergency financial assistance gave Maine schools a valuable tool to help prevent homelessness. But if we want to provide students with the resources to truly succeed, we know more funding is needed.
One of the primary goals of schools statewide is to provide educational stability to children experiencing homelessness, even if their living situation changes. If a student is forced to move from one town to the next, districts work to help them remain at their current school. To do this, our districts sometimes transport students an hour or more each way to the school in their former town.
Our school leaders are committed to this work, but it is expensive. One superintendent in the region estimates their district spends about $1,200 per day in dedicated transportation costs for these students. The state does not help cover these expenses, and only a small amount is covered by the federal government. LD 193 would provide meaningful funding to assist our districts with these costs.
Schools across Maine have also developed an array of wraparound services to help McKinney-Vento students succeed. For instance, educators and social workers help children and families navigate a maze of government bureaucracy to obtain basic social supports, like health insurance and SNAP benefits. This kind of support helps them get to graduation.
On behalf of the Bangor City Council, the Bangor School Department and City residents, we urge you to pass LD 193 to address the growing strain on school budgets as we work to provide the resources needed to serve our homeless student population.
Cara Pelletier, City Council Chair, cara.pelletier@bangormaine.gov Debbie Laurie, City Manager, debbie.laurie@bangormaine.gov

TESTIMONY OF GLBTQ LEGAL ADVOCATES & DEFENDERS IN SUPPORT OF LD 193, AN ACT TO FUND STUDENTS IN MAINE SCHOOLS WHO ARE EXPERIENCING HOMELESSNESS Committee on Education & Cultural Affairs February 26, 2025
Dear Senate Chair Rafferty, House Chair Murphy, and Distinguished Members of the Committee on Education & Cultural Affairs,
GLBTQ Legal Advocates & Defenders (GLAD Law) is a nonprofit legal organization that works in New England and nationally to create a just society free of discrimination based on gender identity and expression, HIV status, and sexual orientation. We appreciate the opportunity to submit this testimony in Support of LD 193, An Act to Fund Students in Maine Schools Who Are Experiencing Homelessness.
In the 2023 Maine Integrated Youth Health Survey, 2.6 percent of high school respondents reported experiencing housing instability in the previous 30 days alone.1 Rates were higher for students of color and for LGBTQ students.2
While these students represent a small overall percentage of the student population in Maine, many of them experience heightened needs and barriers to accessing education. Students experiencing homelessness have a higher rate of chronic absenteeism than their peers, with national data showing a rate of 48 percent.3 And they have a lower graduation rate than their peers - just 60 percent of Maine students experiencing homelessness graduated high school in four years, compared to 86 percent of all students.4 That lower graduation rate in turn puts young people at greater risk of homelessness later in life, underscoring the important role that obtaining education plays in supporting economic wellbeing.5 Young people who are not in school can also have interactions with law enforcement and become involved with the juvenile justice system.

1 Maine Department of Health and Human Services (DHHS) & Maine Department of Education (DOE), Maine: 2023 MIYHS High School Report 949, https://www.maine.gov/miyhs/sites/default/files/2023_Reports/Detailed_Reports/HS/MIYHS2023_Detailed_ Reports_HS_State/Maine%20High%20School%20Detailed%20Tables.pdf 2 Id. at 950-51. 33 School House Connection, 2025 Fact Sheet: Educating Children and Youth Experiencing Homelessness 2 (2025), https://schoolhouseconnection.org/wp-content/uploads/2025/02/Educating-Children-and-YouthExperiencing-Homelessness-2025-Fact-Sheet.pdf. 4 Maine Children's Alliance, 2023 Maine Kids Count 43, https://mainechildrensalliance.org/site/assets/files/2024/2023_kidscount_databook_interactive.pdf. 5 School House Connection, 2025 Fact Sheet: Educating Children and Youth Experiencing Homelessness 2 (2025), https://schoolhouseconnection.org/wp-content/uploads/2025/02/Educating-Children-and-YouthExperiencing-Homelessness-2025-Fact-Sheet.pdf.

GLBTQ Legal Advocates & Defenders | 18 Tremont St, STE 950 Boston, MA 02108

gladlaw.org

There are a range of actions schools can take to promote educational attainment and the overall health and wellbeing of students experiencing homelessness. While the federal McKinney-Vento Act establishes some measures that districts must take to support these students, such as ensuring transportation, permitting student enrollment even without required documents, and designating a homeless education liaison, the Act is insufficient to ensure that students in housing crisis can consistently attend and succeed in school. This bill would help to address that gap by increasing the funding available to schools for each student experiencing homelessness in the school population. Schools are essential both in delivering services that help meet the immediate needs of students experiencing homelessness and setting them up for stability and success in the future - but they cannot do so without sufficient resources. Accordingly, GLAD Law strongly supports this bill.
Sincerely, Hannah Hussey Staff Attorney Mary Bonauto Senior Director of Civil Rights and Legal Strategies GLBTQ Legal Advocates & Defenders Portland, Maine

Before the Joint Standing Committee on Education & Cultural Affairs In Favor of LD 193 - An Act to Fund Students in Maine Schools Who Are Experiencing
Homelessness
Greetings, Senator Rafferty, Representative Murphy, and Members of the Joint Standing Committee on Education & Cultural Affairs,
My name is Jared Gay, and I am the Director of Public Policy and Advocacy at United Way of Southern Maine (UWSM). Thank you for the opportunity to provide testimony in strong support of LD 193.
United Way of Southern Maine works to ensure that every person in our community has the opportunity to thrive--starting with access to quality education, stable housing, and financial stability. We focus specifically on supporting ALICE households--Asset Limited, Income Constrained, Employed--families who are working, often multiple jobs, but still cannot afford the basics. Many ALICE families live paycheck to paycheck, just one unexpected expense away from crisis. For these families, housing instability and homelessness are very real threats, and for their children, those challenges follow them into the classroom every day.
LD 193 would provide a modest but critical adjustment to the school funding formula-- adding a 0.50 weight for each student identified as experiencing homelessness. For ALICE students and families, this change could make a meaningful difference. It would enable school districts to deliver the supports these students need to succeed--transportation, trauma-informed care, tutoring, case management, and access to food and hygiene supplies.
ALICE children experiencing homelessness are more likely to struggle with attendance, academic performance, and social-emotional wellbeing. They may lack a quiet place to do homework, internet access for virtual learning, or consistent meals outside of school. Educators and schools in our region are doing heroic work to support these students, but they are being asked to do more with less. LD 193 would acknowledge these challenges and equip schools with the funding they need to meet the moment.
This legislation is not only a recognition of the growing number of Maine students experiencing homelessness--it is also a commitment to ensuring that homelessness does

not dictate a child's future. We must invest in the potential of every student, including those who face the steepest odds.
Thank you for the opportunity to testify.

Testimony in Support of LD 193
February 26, 2025
Chair Rafferty, Chair Murphy, and Distinguished Members of the Education and Cultural Affairs
Committee:
Thank you for the opportunity to testify today in strong support of LD 193, which would
establish a weighted count for students experiencing homelessness in the Essential Programs and Services funding formula.
As the superintendent serving the communities of Biddeford, Saco, and Dayton, I witness firsthand the unique and significant challenges faced by our homeless student population. These
challenges not only impact the students themselves but create additional responsibilities for our school districts that are currently unrecognized in our funding fonnula.
The Growing Crisis of Student Homelessness
In recent years, we have seen a concerning increase in student homelessness across our districts.
This is not merely a housing issue----it represents a complex educational challenge that requires specialized resources and support systems. Students experiencing homelessness face numerous
obstacles to educational success, including:
Inconsistent attendance and higher mobility between schools
Lack of quiet spaces for homework and studying
Limited access to basic necessities like food, clothing, and hygiene supplies Heightened emotional and psychological stress
Difficulty participating in extracurricular activities
Challenges with transportation to and from school
These obstacles lead to higher rates of substance use and abuse, high-risk behaviors, engagement with law enforcement, imprisonment, and drastically higher rates of dropping out of school.
Classrooms, schools, and districts with high levels of homelessness must program differently and provide a higher level of support than is typically needed. The concentration of homeless students in certain schools creates unique challenges that require specialized approaches to instruction, social-emotional support, and family engagement. These needs extend beyond what our standard educational programs can address without additional resources.
A Fiscally Responsible Approach to a Growing Challenge

The current ED 279 funding fonnula does not adequately account for these challenges. While we
havemechanisms to recognize additional needs for economically disadvantaged students,
English language leamers, and special education students, we have no such acknowledgment for homeless students who often require even more intensive supports.
This is not about expanding govemment, but rather about making smart investments now that
will reduce long-term costs to our communities and state. Without proper educational support, homeless students are more likely to require expensive interventions later through social services, healthcare, public safety, and corrections systems.
'
In practice, our districts must divert resources from other areas to provide:
0 Additional transportation services beyond standard routes and thousands of person-hours and tens of thousands of road miles transporting homeless students Specialized staff training on trauma-informed teaching practices Extended day programming and academic support services Coordination with social services and community organizations
Basic necessity supplies that other students would typically have at home
Mental health supports and counseling services
Why a 0.50 Weight Makes Practical Sense
The proposed 0.50 weight in LD 193 is both reasonable and necessary. It recognizes that serving
homeless students requires approximately 50% more resources than serving housed students with similar academic profiles. This additional weighting would help sustain the critical services we
already provide to homeless students, which include:
0 Extended transportation services beyond regular routes to ensure consistent attendance, often requiring specialized arrangements to accommodate temporary housing locations
0 Comprehensive mental health and counseling supports to address trauma and instability experienced by homeless students
0 Food security programs including weekend backpacks, extended meal programs, and connections to community food resources
0 Housing navigation assistance for families, helping them access shelters, transitional housing, and permanent housing opportunities
0 Provision of basic necessities including clothing, hygiene supplies, school materials, and other items that housed students typically have readily available
0 Extended learning opportunities and academic interventions to address gaps caused by high mobility and attendance challenges
Accountability and Results-Focused Approach
This proposal is not about simply spending more money. It's about ensuring accountability in our
educational system by properly aligning resources with demonstrated needs. By incorporating this weighted count into the EPS formula, we create transparency around these expenses and can
better measure outcomes against investments.
Furthermore, this change would bring stability and predictability to district budgeting. Currently,
we experience significant fluctuations as our homeless population changes, often unpredictably.

Having a weighted count would allow us to plan more effectively and ensure consistent services regardless of population shifts.
A Maine Solution to a Maine Problem
This legislation is about local control and empowering communities to address their specific challenges. School districts across our state-----rural, suburban, and urban alike--are seeing increases in student homelessness. This weighted count would provide districts the flexibility to develop solutions that Work for their unique circumstances without mandating specific programs.
Conclusion
Now is the time for action. Our homeless student populations continue to grow, and the resources
required to serve them effectively continue to strain our budgets. The proposed 0.50 weight represents a fair and reasonable adjustment to reflect the true cost of educating these vulnerable
students.
This should not be a partisan issue. Both sides of the aisle can agree that investing in education that leads to self-sufficiency and productivity is fiscally responsible and morally right.
Supporting LD 193 reflects our shared Maine values of personal responsibility, community
support, and creating pathways to independence and success.
It is also a statement that we understand and value the hard work of Maine educators who are on
the front lines supporting the needs of our changing communities and the struggles that families face. Every day, teachers, counselors, and staff go above and beyond to ensure homeless students can succeed despite their circumstances. This legislation acknowledges their dedication and provides them with the resources they need to continue this essential work.
I urge the committee to support LD 193. This legislation would create a more equitable funding
system that recognizes the real challenges faced by districts with significant homeless populations. Most importantly, it would help ensure that all Maine students, regardless of their housing status, have access to the educational opportunities they deserve and the chance to become productive, taxpaying citizens of our state.
Thank you for your consideration of this important issue. I would be happy to answer any
questions or provide additional information that might assist the committee in its deliberations.
Respectful ubmitted,

Good afternoon, Chair Rafferty and Co-Chair Pierce, and Committee Members of the Education and Cultural Affairs Committee,
My name is Julie Orrego, and I am the Advocacy Supervisor at Preble Street. Our mission is to provide accessible, barrier-free services to empower people experiencing homelessness, housing, hunger, and poverty and advocate for solutions to these problems. Preble Street's Joe Kreisler Teen Shelter is one of four shelters for homeless youth in Maine. Youth who utilize the Joe Kreisler Teen Shelter connect with caseworkers to meet their basic needs and access other services, such as health care, employment, housing, and education.
Every day, Preble Street sees the challenges that students experiencing homelessness or housing insecurity face, like moving from one school district to another, living in unsafe conditions or an unstable family situation, and lacking things like weather-appropriate clothing, medical care, transportation, technology, and even prescription glasses. Many young people have experienced extensive trauma. For many youths, school is a safe space.
Preble Street strongly supports LD 193 because it helps ensure that every student can succeed academically, regardless of their housing status. This bill specifies that the .05 added weight to a school's budget for each student experiencing homelessness can be used for students in grades K-12. This will support youth of all ages who may be experiencing homelessness or housing insecurity. Far too many youths in our state face the monumental burden and challenge of homelessness. According to the 2024 Point in Time Count, 19.5% of all households experiencing homelessness had at least one child (under 18). This bill will provide critical additional resources and support for students to succeed.
Preble Street urges you to pass this legislation because it invests in a better future for young people in our state. Every student deserves the opportunity to achieve their full potential without having their socioeconomic status standing in the way.

Testimony of Rep. Kristen Cloutier in support of
LD 193, An Act to Fund Students in Maine Schools Who Are Experiencing Homelessness
Before the Joint Standing Committee on Education and Cultural Affairs
Senator Rafferty, Representative Murphy and distinguished members of the Education and Cultural Affairs Committee, my name is Kristen Cloutier, and I represent House District 94, which includes part of my hometown of Lewiston. I am pleased to submit this testimony in support of LD 193, An Act to Fund Students in Maine Schools Who Are Experiencing Homelessness.
I want to thank Rep. Marshall Archer for sponsoring this critical legislation. This bill addresses an urgent need in our educational system that has only grown more pressing in recent years.
In the 2022-23 school year, 4,400 students were identified in Maine as experiencing homelessness - a number that has almost doubled from previous years. This alarming increase highlights the growing crisis that these vulnerable young people face.
LD 193 proposes a necessary amendment to the school funding formula to provide additional resources specifically targeted to support students experiencing homelessness. These students face unique challenges that require specialized support services to ensure they can access the education they deserve.
Students experiencing housing insecurity often struggle with inconsistent attendance, difficulty completing assignments and challenges focusing on academics while managing basic survival needs. By providing dedicated funding through this legislation, we can help schools develop targeted interventions to address these barriers to learning.
The proposed funding would enable schools to provide essential support services, including transportation assistance, academic support, access to school supplies and coordination with community resources to help stabilize these students' lives.
I urge the committee to consider the profound impact this legislation could have on Maine's most vulnerable students and to support its passage.
Thank you for your consideration.

Good afternoon, Sen. Rafferty, Rep. Murphy and members of the Education and Cultural Affairs
Committee. My name is Marshall Archer, and I represent House District 129, which is part of
Saco.
Thank you for being here today to discuss an issue that strikes at the core of our commitment to
equity in education, ensuring that students experiencing homelessness receive the support they
need to tlnive in Maine's schools.
Today, I am proud to introduce LD 193, An Act to Fund Students in Maine Schools Who Are
Experiencing Homelessness, a bill that will provide dedicated funding using Maine's Essential Programs and Services (EPS) formula to better support our most vulnerable students.

From lacking stable housing to struggling with food insecurity and transportation, these students
are at greater risk of falling behind academically and disengaging from their education altogether. According to recent data, thousands of Maine students face housing instability each year. This is not just an education issue--it is a community crisis.

When we invest in these students, we invest in Maine's future. We empower young people to
break cycles of poverty and instability, helping them graduate, pursue higher education or vocational training and contribute meaningfully to our communities.

Maine Mayors Coalition Testimony on LD 193
An Act to Fund Students in Maine Schools Who Are Experiencing Homelessness
Senator Rafferty, Representative Murphy and distinguished members of the ]oint Standing Committee on Education and Cultural Affairs, the Maine Mayors Coalition is providing
testimony in support of LD 193, An Act to Fund Students in Maine Schools Who Are
Experiencing Homelessness.
The Maine Mayors Coalition is a nonpartisan group representing the mayors of eleven Maine communities -- Auburn, Bangor, Biddeford, Lewiston, Portland, Rockland, Saco, Sanford, South Portland, Waterville and Westbrook - and nearly 300,000 residents. The Coalition advocates on behalf of our citizens and municipalities for policies that recognize the vital services Maine cities provide and the positive impact Maine cities have on our state. The Coalition seeks to work in partnership with state and federal elected officials to meet the needs of Maine people.
One of our most important obligations as public officials is to our young people -- they are Maine's future. Ensuring they receive the best education possible prepares them to become thriving members of society.
As you're well aware, some municipalities need additional resources to support students who face extraordinary challenges in their lives. One such challenge for a growing number of students is not having basic shelter. Over the last few years, municipalities of all sizes have seen more and more students experiencing homelessness.
Among our Coalition members, Lewiston has 420 unhoused students. Auburn reported 234
for the 2023/2024 school year and expects to meet or exceed that number in this school year. Biddeford has 200 unhoused students, South Portland 180, Saco 150 and Westbrook 122. That totals more than 1,300 unhoused students in just these six cities. Given the state's lack of affordable housing, we expect the numbers will rise, not fall.
We fully support the change to the Essential Programs and Services funding formula
proposed in LD 193 that would give additional weight to a school administrative unit's pupil count for students experiencing homelessness. This change would allow schools to provide the resources needed for unhoused students to access a quality education without placing the additional costs on to property taxpayers.

Thank you for your time and attention.

Testimony of Mayor of the City of Portland, Mark Dion In Support of
LD 193, An Act to Fund Students in Maine Schools Who Are Experiencing Homelessness Before the Joint Standing Committee on Education and Cultural Affairs
Senator Rafferty, Representative Murphy and distinguished members of the Education and Cultural Affairs Committee, my name is Mark Dion, Mayor of Portland and I write to provide testimony in support of LD 193 on behalf of the City of Portland. Nearly 70,000 Mainers call Portland home and approximately 6,000 students attend our seventeen public schools. LD 193 is critical legislation that would address an important need in education.
Over the last four years, the Portland Public Schools has served an average of more than 600 students experiencing homelessness per year - approximately 10 percent of our total student population. In 2020, Portland Public Schools served a total of 420 students; in 2021, we served 353 students; in 2022, we served 846 students; in 2023, we served 823 students; and this school year, as of November 2024, we had already identified over 600 students classified as McKinney-Vento. To illustrate the gravity of the housing challenges in Portland, the district identifies an average of five students every day who are either at risk of becoming homeless or are already experiencing homelessness.
Homelessness creates barriers for students in accessing and succeeding in their education. With the housing crisis in Portland, unfortunately, many families have to find housing in other towns which may not have the appropriate services that are found in Portland. In some cases, families have been moved from one shelter to another or one hotel to another. There are also families who sleep in very temporary shelters, such as a church. This type of shelter is only for sleeping and availability changes everyday. Any one of these situations contributes to unstable school attendance, arriving late for school, difficulty accessing after-school opportunities, social- emotional difficulties, and constant interruption in schooling due to transfers, etc. All of these factors are barriers to educational success and pose challenges for school districts.
The proposed funding in LD 193 would go to the costs associated with to the increasing number of students experiencing homelessness in the past four years. Those costs to PPS in identifying and serving this student population include additional staffing as well as non-personnel costs associated with transportation, supplies, and other services. Personnel expenses have included a full-time Mckinney-Vento liaison, a full-time Mckinney-Vento social worker, and a

L.D. 193, An Act to Fund Students in Maine Who are Experiencing Homelessness proposes changes to
the EPS system that would provide greater financial resources to schools based on their population of students experiencing homelessness. L.D. 193 would grant a new funding weight of .50 per student experiencing homelessness, defined as a student identified by the school administrative unit (SAU) as a
homeless child or youth, as defined by the federal McKinney-Vento Homeless Assistance Act, 42 United States Code Section ll434a.

Students lacking a fixed, regular, and adequate nighttime residence must be identified by an SAU's homeless liaison and data collected in the SAU's Student Information System (SIS) for annual reporting
to the Maine Department of Education (DOE). Identification can occur at any time during the calendar year as homelessness can impact families and youth at any time and effects rural, urban, and suburban areas. Once a student is identified as experiencing homelessness under the Federal McKinney-Vento Homeless Assistance Act, the student carries homeless status in the SIS and has access to McKinneyVento provisions through June 30"` of that school year. Beginning on July I, homeless liaisons at the
SAUs are then tasked with outreach to connect with families previously identified as homeless to
determine if they remain in unstable housing.

The current Essential Programs and Services (EPS) school funding model is designed to fund SAUs based

on the collection of student data and specific demographic criteria on a specific date in time in order to be

able to provide those funds as equitably as possible. Each year the collection of all student data used in

the

It would be difficult to correctly account for and allocate

necessary funds using the EPS formula for the homeless students in Maine, given that students can be

identified at any time during the school year, or transition into stable housing at any time during that school year. Pupil counts conducted on October 1" would not capture an accurate picture of students

experiencing homelessness over the course of the school year.

Maine's commitment to funding 55% of the total state-level cost of education, as opposed to 55% of the district-by-district cost of education, means that making any small change to EPS has ripple-effects that
impact every SAU in the state. By providing additional funding to SAUs that serve a greater percentage
of youth experiencing homelessness, there are other communities in the State that will receive less funding. These decisions must be carefully weighed.

L.D. 193
AN ACT TO FUND STUDENTS IN MAINE SCHOOLS
WHO ARE EXPERIENCING HOMELESSNESS
February 26, 2025
Senator Rafferty, Representative Noonan Murphy and members of the Education and Cultural Affairs
Committee. I am Robbie Feinberg, the director of communications and government relations for Maine
School Management Association, testifying on behalf of the legislative committees of the Maine School Boards Association and Maine School Superintendents Association in support of L.D. 193.
Across Maine, more communities are seeing residents unable to find a permanent place to live, and our
schools sit on the front lines of addressing this challenge.
During the last school year, more than 4,000 Maine students lacked a fixed place to live each night -- doubledup with friendsor staying in a hotel. Every day, our staff see more students enter class without basic needs:
clean clothes, hygiene products, and school supplies.
Our superintendents and school board members are grateful that the legislature has already taken steps to tackle this growing challenge. The recent pilot program sponsored by Sen. Rafferty to provide up to $750 per student for emergency financial assistance gave our schools a valuable tool to help prevent homelessness. But if we want to provide students with the resources to truly succeed, we know more funding is needed.
One of our schools' primary goals is to provide educational stability to children experiencing homelessness, even if their living situation changes. If a student is forced to move from one town to the next, districts work to help them remain at their current school - a place where they've already made friends and developed relationships with staff. To do this, our districts sometimes transport students an hour or more each way to the
school in their former town.
Our school leaders are committed to this work, but it is expensive. One superintendent in central Maine estimates their district spends about $1,200 per day in dedicated_transportation costs for these students. The state does not help to cover these expenses, and only a small amount is covered by the federal government. L.D. 193 would provide meaningful funding to assist our districts with these costs.
Schools across Maine have also developed an array of wraparound services to help our McKinney-Vento students succeed. Educators and social workers help children and families navigate a maze of government
bureaucracy to obtain basic social supports, like health insurance and SNAP benefits. And because students

received additional federal funding for homeless students during the pandemic saw improvement in graduation rates, absenteeism rates, and reading and math scores. Unfortunately, much of that expanded pandemic-era funding has come to an end. L.D. 193 recognizes these students' substantial needs and provides
schools with the resources to make a meaningful difference. We urge you to support this bill.

Valerie Caruso Augusta LD 193
Valerie Caruso As a public education professional with over 30 years of experience working in public education I am very concerned about this issue. According to reports from Maine Public and the Maine Department of Education, the number of homeless students in Maine during the 2022-2023 school year was over 4,400. This number represents a large jump compared to previous years, attributed to a severe lack of affordable housing in the state.
Education is a fundamental right, yet for students experiencing homelessness in Maine, accessing a stable and supportive learning environment can be incredibly challenging. Without financial assistance, these students face significant barriers that hinder their ability to succeed in school. Maine should provide dedicated funding for students experiencing homelessness to ensure they have the resources needed to thrive academically and personally.
First, homelessness creates severe obstacles to academic success. Students without stable housing often struggle with inconsistent attendance, lack of school supplies, and difficulty concentrating due to hunger or stress. According to national studies, students experiencing homelessness are more likely to drop out of school than their housed peers. By providing direct financial support--such as covering transportation, meal programs, and school supplies--Maine can help these students stay in school and maintain their education despite their hardships.
Additionally, funding would provide access to essential services that go beyond academics. Many students facing homelessness lack access to hygiene products, medical care, or a safe place to study. Financial support could help schools connect these students with counselors, healthcare providers, and after-school programs, ensuring their well-being both inside and outside the classroom. When basic needs are met, students can focus on learning instead of worrying about survival.
Some may argue that schools should not be responsible for addressing homelessness, as it is a broader societal issue. However, schools are often the most stable part of a homeless student's life, making them the ideal place to provide support. Investing in these students not only improves their individual futures but also strengthens communities by breaking the cycle of poverty and homelessness.
In conclusion, Maine must fund students experiencing homelessness to give them a fair chance at education and success. By addressing their unique challenges through financial assistance and essential services, the state can ensure that every student--regardless of their housing situation--has the opportunity to learn, grow, and build a brighter future.
